lead: The check-out starts at the check-in: what you write down on Saturday is what the boat is measured against a week later. Your charter contract and the base's briefing set the terms; these notes give the general practice behind them.

sections.title: What is written down cannot be charged later

qa.q: Why should I write every scratch on the charter check-in form?
qa.a: Because the form you sign is the **baseline** for the check-out: a fault recorded as old at check-in is wear, not new damage, and cannot be charged later. Photograph it, and count the inventory before you sign.

blocks.p: The inventory list and the check-in form you sign are the **baseline** for the check-out. Count before you sign: the count can wait for the evening, the signature waits for the count. Whatever is short is written on the list, items promised from the store included; strike them out when they arrive.

A count proves an item is there, not its state. Write down torn seams, a damp mattress or a loose hinge, with photos, and test what you are told works while the technician is aboard. A fault recorded as old at check-in is wear, not new damage.

lines: Catamaran: both hour meters on the form

sections.title: Report it the day it happens

qa.q: What do I do if I damage the charter yacht during the week?
qa.a: Photograph it and phone the base **at once**, the same day. Reported, a chip is a repair on the settlement; hidden, it is found at the check-out anyway and can cost you the damage waiver.

blocks.p: Contracts normally require damage to be reported to the base **at once**. Reported, a chip is a repair on the settlement. Hidden, it is found at the check-out anyway and can cost you the damage waiver. A loss is reported the same way: for lost keys the base can send spares.

blocks.p: If you touch another boat, tell the base before the check-out: it is a third-party claim, which the base reports to the insurer. If another boat hits you and the repair is held from your deposit, have the refund on recovery written on the settlement. At the end hand in a short list of the faults you met: it costs you nothing and helps the next crew.

sections.title: Alongside and fuelled before the deadline

qa.q: What if bad weather stops me returning the charter yacht to the base on time?
qa.a: Call the base the day before, say where you are and decide with their advice: a **late fee** is never a reason to sail into a gale. If they tell you to wait, keep their messages.

fig.note: A first: fill up and keep the receipt. Then B.

blocks.p: 'Back at the base' means alongside on the berth the base gives you, before the time in the contract: call before you enter. Work back from the deadline at motoring speed and leave time for fuel. 22 miles at 6 knots is under four hours; at 2 knots under sail it is eleven. A calm does not excuse a late return.

A gale is different, and a late fee is never a reason to sail into one. Call the base the day before, say where you are and decide with their advice; if they tell you to wait, keep their messages. If you come back early, arrange an early check-out before the crew leave.

The tank normally goes back **full**: keep the receipt and read the fuel clause. Water full and holding tank empty are common check-out items; pump out only where the local rules allow. The last night in the base marina is usually in the charter price.

sections.title: Count, clean and pack before the technician comes

qa.q: What do I need to do the evening before checking out of a charter yacht?
qa.a: Count the inventory against the list, clean the galley, fridge and heads, take food and rubbish ashore, and empty the cabins. **Final cleaning included** rarely covers your rubbish, a dirty fridge or the heads.

blocks.p: Count the inventory against the list the evening before: the boat hook is then found under a berth, not on the settlement. 'Final cleaning included' rarely covers your rubbish, a dirty fridge or the heads. Rinse a stain at once and show it in the morning.

sections.title: Go round with the technician, phone in hand

qa.q: How do I avoid unfair damage charges at the charter check-out inspection?
qa.a: Be at the **walk-round** with your dated check-in photos and answer each point on the spot. Dispute a charge at the base before you sign, and sign only the completed form, never a blank one.

lines: Check-in form and your photo: 1 371 h
Form says 1 421: corrected before you sign

blocks.p: Be there for the walk-round and see each point as it is found: you can answer on the spot with a dated check-in photo. New damage is settled against the check-in form and photos, so ask to see the diver's photo too. Read the hour meter and the fuel gauge with the technician. Rotten stitching is **wear and tear**, which contracts normally do not charge.

A charge is disputed at the base, before you sign. Sign only the completed form, after the inspection, never a blank one, and keep a copy. Then photograph the signed form, the hull, the fuel gauge and the hour meter. If nobody can inspect before you must leave, have the office sign a timed note: returned, not yet inspected.

qa.q: How does an excess per incident work on a yacht charter damage waiver?
qa.a: An **excess per incident** caps each repair separately: with a €500 excess, a €350 chip costs €350 and a €900 repair costs €500, so €850 comes off the deposit, not €1,250.

blocks.p: Lost inventory is normally charged at the base's price list, and a waiver seldom covers it. Ask for an itemised settlement, a receipt for every deduction and the date the card hold is released. Never settle damage in cash without paper. A cash deposit comes back against the receipt you were given at check-in.

An **excess per incident** caps each repair separately. If the hold is still on your card weeks later, write to the base with the signed form: only the base can cancel it early. A clean signed check-out form is your answer to a charge raised after other crews have sailed the boat: refuse it in writing. In a review give facts; a dispute goes to the base in writing.
